title: Watch the Completely Unsafe, Vertigo-Inducing Footage of Workers Building New York’s Iconic Skyscrapers
description:
in History |   	September 2nd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Would any­one in their right mind sign up for a job that had a high risk of mortality
body:
in History |   	September 2nd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Would any­one in their right mind sign up for a job that had a high risk of mortality/disability? Or a job where red hot met­al is being hurled direct­ly at your face? Back in the 1920s this was the lot of the men who built New York’s sky­line, the men who con­struct­ed the Chrysler Build­ing and the Empire State, giant phal­lic sym­bols of America’s bur­geon­ing wealth and pow­er.
In this short clip (remas­tered and quite decent­ly col­orized) from the Smith­son­ian Chan­nel, we get a brief glimpse of the per­ils encoun­tered dai­ly on the build­ing site. Nick­named “rough­necks,” the nar­ra­tor points out that they work with­out har­ness­es, safe­ty ropes, or hard hats. Red hot riv­ets are thrown at men on the met­al beams high­er up and they are meant to catch them with what looks like a tin fun­nel. You can see the thinnest of ropes used to lift the now-icon­ic stain­less steel art-deco eagles into place by men wear­ing felt hats and no gloves.
The work­ers came from Europe, many who had trained on ships. Some came from Montreal’s Kah­nawake reser­va­tion. The lat­ter, known as Iron Walk­ers, were Mohawk, known for work­ing fear­less­ly at great heights.
“A lot of peo­ple think Mohawks aren’t afraid of heights; that’s not true,” Kyle Karon­hi­ak­tatie Beau­vais said in 2002. “We have as much fear as the next guy. The dif­fer­ence is that we deal with it bet­ter.”
Much of this work was doc­u­ment­ed by pho­tog­ra­ph­er Lewis Hine, who cap­tured a mix of brute strength and grav­i­ty-defy­ing courage along with pri­vate moments of rest, catch­ing a smoke or tak­ing lunch. You can see many of his famous pho­tos in this clip:


	

The Chrysler Build­ing was com­plet­ed in 1930, and reached a height of 1,046 feet (319 m), fea­tur­ing 77 floors. It held its fame as the world’s tallest build­ing for only 11 months. In 1931 work­ers com­plet­ed the Empire State Build­ing, stand­ing at 1,454 feet (443.2 m) and hous­ing 102 floors. (That’s dinky com­pared to the cur­rent record-hold­er: Dubai’s Burj Khal­i­fa, which stands at 2,722 feet (829.8 m)).
Heads up: The Smith­son­ian Chan­nel clip has some of the worst exam­ples of YouTube com­ments among the videos we’ve high­light­ed over the years, as if peo­ple still don’t work in ter­ri­ble and unsafe con­di­tions in order to feed their fam­i­lies and pay rent. And look! Here’s a guy who walks out onto the Chrysler eagle just for fun. Don’t say we didn’t warn you:


	

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

title: How Phone Addiction Keeps You from Achieving a Productive “Flow State”
description:
in Life, Technology |   	September 1st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

If you have an iPhone, try push­ing its side but­ton three times in a row. J
body:
in Life, Technology |   	September 1st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

If you have an iPhone, try push­ing its side but­ton three times in a row. Just like mag­ic, the screen should turn from col­or into black-and-white, or rather grayscale. (To do the same on an Android phone, you’ll have to dive into set­tings, then “acces­si­bil­i­ty,” “vision enhance­ments,” and “col­or cor­rec­tion.”) Why would you want that in the first place? As Har­vard Kennedy School and Har­vard Busi­ness School pro­fes­sor Arthur C. Brooks explains in the Big Think video above, “one of the ways that you can actu­al­ly get less hooked by social media, or any screen-based tech­nol­o­gy, is by turn­ing off the col­or.” When you get only black, white, and the shades of gray in between, “you will care less about your screen, and you will look at it less.”
This may ring true to those of us who remem­ber pure­ly mono­chro­mat­ic cell­phones, and how lit­tle time we spent star­ing at them. But no mat­ter your gen­er­a­tion, Brooks has plen­ty of use­ful advice about how to break the depen­den­cy on your phone from which, as a twen­ty-first-cen­tu­ry inter­net user, you almost cer­tain­ly suf­fer.
“You notice when some­body is addict­ed to hero­in, because it’s not that com­mon for ordi­nary peo­ple,” he says. “You don’t notice when some­body’s addict­ed to their phone, because lit­er­al­ly every­body is addict­ed to their phones.” There­fore, we could all ben­e­fit from turn­ing off noti­fi­ca­tions, set­ting defined “tech times,” exer­cis­ing with­out our devices, and going on mul­ti-day med­i­ta­tion retreats — though we may have to work up to that last one.
The func­tion­al phone addict may believe that all his dai­ly scrolling may not have that much of a neg­a­tive impact on his life, and even that it helps him unwind. What he does­n’t real­ize, in Brooks’ view, is the extent to which dig­i­tal dis­trac­tions keep him out of what psy­chol­o­gist Mihaly Csik­szent­mi­ha­lyi called “flow.” (These com­ments come around the 27:06 mark.) Flow hap­pens “when you’re involved immer­sive­ly in some­thing, and hours turn to min­utes. You lose track of time. It’s intense­ly plea­sur­able,” almost “like a state of Bud­dhist med­i­ta­tion.” Con­scious­ly or uncon­scious­ly, we use our phones and oth­er dig­i­tal devices in a way that pre­vents flow, “mul­ti­task­ing” between numer­ous tasks and dis­trac­tions, nev­er pay­ing sus­tained atten­tion to any one thing. At the root of this impulse is a fear of bore­dom, which must be endured in order to accom­plish any­thing mean­ing­ful. The irony of our new­found abil­i­ty to evade bore­dom every moment is that, if we do so, the whole of life turns out to be pret­ty bor­ing.

title: How Leonardo da Vinci’s Procrastination Contributed to His Creativity
description:
in History, Psychology |   	September 2nd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
At the height of their pro­duc­tiv­i­ty as Bea­t­les, nei­ther Paul McCart­ne
body:
in History, Psychology |   	September 2nd, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
At the height of their pro­duc­tiv­i­ty as Bea­t­les, nei­ther Paul McCart­ney nor John Lennon could read or write music nota­tion. Clear­ly it did­n’t keep them from mak­ing a cul­tur­al impact, and as with so much else in life, they regard­ed it humor­ous­ly. As McCart­ney has said, they used to liken them­selves to ancient Egypt­ian pharaohs, who relied on scribes rather than being lit­er­ate them­selves. It’s worth con­sid­er­ing whether, all things con­sid­ered, this inabil­i­ty was real­ly a defi­cien­cy: not being rig­or­ous­ly schooled in the tra­di­tions and con­ven­tions of music could have giv­en them just the free­dom they need­ed to cre­ate fresh songs. And if you’ve strug­gled with pro­cras­ti­na­tion, have you con­sid­ered liken­ing your­self to Leonar­do da Vin­ci?
“Leonar­do’s dif­fi­cul­ties with stick­ing to tasks were per­va­sive from child­hood,” says a Sci­enceDai­ly sum­ma­ry of a 2019 paper by clin­i­cal neu­ro­sci­en­tist Mar­co Catani. “Accounts from biog­ra­phers and con­tem­po­raries show Leonar­do was con­stant­ly on the go, often jump­ing from task to task.” Regard­ing his life at a dis­tance of half a mil­len­ni­um, we may con­sid­er Leonar­do not just a genius but a high­ly pro­duc­tive one, with a body of work includ­ing numer­ous inven­tions built and unbuilt as well as paint­ings like Lady with an Ermine, The Last Sup­per, and the Mona Lisa — which near­ly joined the man’s pile of aban­doned projects. As Nico­las Cole writes at Inc., schol­ar­ship sug­gests that Leonar­do “paint­ed the Mona Lisa on and off for a few years start­ing in 1503, left it unfin­ished, and didn’t com­plete it until close to his death in 1519.”
“While paint­ing The Last Sup­per, Leonar­do would some­times stare at the work for an hour, final­ly make one small stroke, and then leave,” writes Wal­ter Isaac­son in his biog­ra­phy Leonar­do da Vin­ci. His expla­na­tion: “Men of lofty genius some­times accom­plish the most when they work least, for their minds are occu­pied with their ideas and the per­fec­tion of their con­cep­tions, to which they after­wards give form.” When the non-Renais­sance men of the world say things like that, it comes off as self-aggran­diz­ing excuse-mak­ing. Many, per­haps most of us have spent so much time telling our­selves we’re prepar­ing for a task that it just became anoth­er means of pro­cras­ti­na­tion. But “pro­cras­ti­nat­ing like Leonar­do requires work: it involves gath­er­ing all the pos­si­ble facts and ideas, and only after that allow­ing the col­lec­tion to sim­mer,” notes Isaac­son.
Not that the patrons frus­trat­ed by Leonar­do’s fail­ures to deliv­er could always keep that in mind. After he worked at the Vat­i­can for three years, Pope Leo X dis­missed him with the judg­ment that he would nev­er accom­plish any­thing, “for he begins by think­ing of the end of the work, before the begin­ning.” Even Leonar­do him­self made a deathbed apol­o­gy “to God and Man for leav­ing so much undone.” Hav­ing exam­ined the nature of both Leonar­do’s chal­lenges and his bril­liance, Catani comes to the con­clu­sion that he exhib­it­ed traits con­sis­tent with a con­di­tion only giv­en a name well with­in liv­ing mem­o­ry, Atten­tion Deficit Hyper­ac­tiv­i­ty Dis­or­der (ADHD). When we find our­selves com­pul­sive­ly flee­ing from the incom­plete work at hand, we’d do well to bear in mind not just Leonar­do’s exam­ple, but also the words of apho­rist Aaron Haspel: “We all suf­fer from a clus­ter of psy­cho­log­i­cal dis­or­ders; it used to be known as per­son­al­i­ty.”

title: Milton Glaser’s 10 Rules for Life & Work: The Celebrated Designer Dispenses Wisdom Gained Over His Long Life & Career
description:
in Creativity, Design, Life |   	September 1st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	
	

“None of us has real­ly the abil­i­ty to under­stand our path unti
body:
in Creativity, Design, Life |   	September 1st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	
	

“None of us has real­ly the abil­i­ty to under­stand our path until it’s over,” the cel­e­brat­ed graph­ic design­er Mil­ton Glaser mused less than a minute into the above video.
The late Mil­ton Glaser’s many con­tri­bu­tions to pop culture—the I ❤ NY logo, the psy­che­del­ic por­trait of a rain­bow-haired Bob Dylan, DC Comics’ clas­sic bul­let logo—con­ferred unde­ni­able author­i­ty. To the out­side eye, he seemed to have a pret­ty firm han­dle on the path he trav­eled for lo those many decades. Aspi­rant design­ers would do well to give extra con­sid­er­a­tion to any advice he might have shared.
As would the rest of us.
His “Ten Things I Have Learned,” orig­i­nal­ly deliv­ered as part of a talk to the AIGA—a ven­er­a­ble mem­ber­ship orga­ni­za­tion for design professionals—qualifies as sol­id life advice of gen­er­al inter­est.
Yes, the Inter­net spawns bul­let-point­ed tips for bet­ter liv­ing the way spring rains yield mush­rooms, but Glaser, a self-described “child of mod­ernism,” did not truck in pithy Insta­gram-friend­ly apho­risms. Instead, his list was born of reflec­tion on the var­i­ous turns of a long and most­ly sat­is­fy­ing cre­ative career.
We’ve excerpt­ed some of his most essen­tial points below, and sug­gest that those read­ers who are still in train­ing give spe­cial empha­sis to num­ber sev­en. Don’t place too much weight on num­ber nine until you’ve estab­lished a sol­id work eth­ic. (See num­ber four for more on that.)
MILTON GLASER”S TEN RULES FOR WORK AND LIFE (& A BONUS JOKE ABOUT A RABBIT).
1. YOU CAN ONLY WORK FOR PEOPLE THAT YOU LIKE
Some years ago I real­ized that… all the work I had done that was mean­ing­ful and sig­nif­i­cant came out of an affec­tion­ate rela­tion­ship with a client.
2. IF YOU HAVE A CHOICE NEVER HAVE A JOB
Here, Glaser quotes com­pos­er John Cage: Nev­er have a job, because if you have a job some­day some­one will take it away from you and then you will be unpre­pared for your old age. 
3. SOME PEOPLE ARE TOXIC AVOID THEM.
Glaser rec­om­mends putting a ques­tion­able com­pan­ion to a gestalt ther­a­py test. If, after spend­ing time with that per­son “you are more tired, then you have been poi­soned. If you have more ener­gy, you have been nour­ished. The test is almost infal­li­ble and I sug­gest that you use it for the rest of your life.”
4. PROFESSIONALISM IS NOT ENOUGH (or THE GOOD IS THE ENEMY OF THE GREAT)
Glaser con­cedes that a record of depend­able excel­lence is some­thing to look for in a brain sur­geon or auto mechan­ic, but for those in the arts, “con­tin­u­ous trans­gres­sion” is the qual­i­ty to cul­ti­vate. Pro­fes­sion­al­ism does not allow for that because trans­gres­sion has to encom­pass the pos­si­bil­i­ty of fail­ure and if you are pro­fes­sion­al your instinct is not to fail, it is to repeat suc­cess. 
5. LESS IS NOT NECESSARILY MORE
I have an alter­na­tive to the propo­si­tion that I believe is more appro­pri­ate. ‘Just enough is more.’
6. STYLE IS NOT TO BE TRUSTED
Style change is usu­al­ly linked to eco­nom­ic fac­tors, as all of you know who have read Marx. Also fatigue occurs when peo­ple see too much of the same thing too often.
7. HOW YOU LIVE CHANGES YOUR BRAIN
The brain is the most respon­sive organ of the body…. Thought changes our life and our behav­ior. I also believe that draw­ing works in the same way…. Draw­ing also makes you atten­tive. It makes you pay atten­tion to what you are look­ing at, which is not so easy.
8. DOUBT IS BETTER THAN CERTAINTY
One of the signs of a dam­aged ego is absolute cer­tain­ty. Schools encour­age the idea of not com­pro­mis­ing and defend­ing your work at all costs. Well, the issue at work is usu­al­ly all about the nature of com­pro­mise…. Ide­al­ly, mak­ing every­one win through acts of accom­mo­da­tion is desir­able.
9. IT DOESN’T MATTER
Glaser cred­its essay­ist Roger Rosenblatt’s Rules for Aging (misiden­ti­fy­ing the title as Aging Grace­ful­ly) with help­ing him artic­u­late his phi­los­o­phy here.  It doesn’t mat­ter what you think. It does not mat­ter if you are late or ear­ly, if you are here or there, if you said it or didn’t say it, if you are clever or if you were stu­pid. If you were hav­ing a bad hair day or a no hair day or if your boss looks at you cock­eyed or your boyfriend or girl­friend looks at you cock­eyed, if you are cock­eyed. If you don’t get that pro­mo­tion or prize or house or if you do – it doesn’t mat­ter.
10. TELL THE TRUTH
It’s inter­est­ing to observe that in the new AIGA’s code of ethics there is a sig­nif­i­cant amount of use­ful infor­ma­tion about appro­pri­ate behav­ior towards clients and oth­er design­ers, but not a word about a designer’s rela­tion­ship to the pub­lic. If we were licensed, telling the truth might become more cen­tral to what we do.
BONUS JOKE
A butch­er was open­ing his mar­ket one morn­ing and as he did a rab­bit popped his head through the door. The butch­er was sur­prised when the rab­bit inquired ‘Got any cab­bage?’ The butch­er said ‘This is a meat mar­ket – we sell meat, not veg­eta­bles.’ The rab­bit hopped off. The next day the butch­er is open­ing the shop and sure enough the rab­bit pops his head round and says ‘You got any cab­bage?’ The butch­er now irri­tat­ed says ‘Lis­ten you lit­tle rodent, I told you yes­ter­day we sell meat, we do not sell veg­eta­bles and the next time you come here I am going to grab you by the throat and nail those flop­py ears to the floor.’ The rab­bit dis­ap­peared hasti­ly and noth­ing hap­pened for a week. Then one morn­ing the rab­bit popped his head around the cor­ner and said ‘Got any nails?’ The butch­er said ‘No.’ The rab­bit said ‘Ok. Got any cab­bage?’’
Read Mil­ton Glaser’s “Ten Things I Have Learned” in its entire­ty here.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

title: Dappled Light and Hazy Shadows Characterize Clio Sze To's Dynamic Paintings
description: Clio Sze To paints in the same way she walks around her home in Paris. Setting out with an open agenda and allowing her route to evolve organicall
body:
Clio Sze To paints in the same way she walks around her home in Paris. Setting out with an open agenda and allowing her route to evolve organically, the artist meanders through the city with an eye toward the patterns and textures that comprise the landscape. When she returns to the studio, the sights transform into impressionistic pieces that capture the feeling of a contemplative hour spent on foot.
In her forthcoming solo exhibition Échos, Sze To presents a suite of oil paintings based on photos she captures on her walks, which become fodder for her stylized composites. Passersby appear in several scenes, although the changing seasons and time of day are a central focus for the artist. The shifting light of dusk, the hazy glow of street lamps, and the dance of shadows as the sun filters through a tree’s canopy are dynamic influences on the urban landscape.
Detail of “Untitled” (2026)
Bulles, or bubbles, was the first title Sze To settled on for this body of work because of the way the thin, translucent membrane can capture and reflect light as a chromatic prism. “Échos, by contrast, implies an outside: something that travels outward, rebounds, and returns to us transformed, rather than a space sealed in upon itself,” a statement says. 
Échos is on view from September 4 to October 10 at Crèvecœur in Paris. Find more from the artist on the gallery’s website.

title: Hans Op de Beeck Taps into Memory, Time, and Enigma in 'Vanishing Point'
description: From the stillness of a lily-specked pond to a nostalgic carousel perched on top of a spindly stand, Hans Op de Beeck’s latest works delve further
body:
From the stillness of a lily-specked pond to a nostalgic carousel perched on top of a spindly stand, Hans Op de Beeck’s latest works delve further into a realm of meditation and solitude. His forthcoming solo exhibition, Vanishing Point at Almine Rech, highlights his characteristically monochromatic sculptures, which he often coats in matte gray. Many are life-size, inviting viewers to stand quietly near a calm figure seated on a chaise lounge beside a fawn or peer into a framed seascape in which definition is only wrought by contrasts in light and shadow.
Scale, lifelike detail, and an array of objects, figures, and animals in different settings lend Op de Beeck’s sculptures a kind of wünderkammer quality when displayed together. Individually, the pieces read like muted curiosities or components of an unusual puzzle. There’s a sense that at any moment, especially in works like “Orrery (Loss),” the scene may whir into motion and transform into the full vibrancy of reality (one might recall the effect in The Wizard of Oz).
“Cécile” (2026), mixed-media, life-size sculpture and “Seascape” (2022), polyester, metal, and coating
Without color, we’re drawn to the dimensionality and textures of reliefs and in-the-round objects, although the tableaux themselves remain enigmatic. We recognize familiar elements, but they seem out of place or in uncanny relationships. Op de Beeck prompts us to imagine how the scenes may have come to be and how they relate to the surroundings, including us. “His art does not explain—it suggests,” the gallery says.
The title of the show is derived from the artistic term “vanishing point,” which describes the effect where all lines converge in a perspective drawing and elements disappear into the distance. A statement says, “Op de Beeck uses it as a metaphor for those moments when the concrete and rational give way to something less tangible—memory, imagination, introspection, or the feeling of briefly slipping outside time.”
Vanishing Point opens on September 10 and continues through November 7 in Brussels. See more on the artist’s Instagram.

title: Watercolors by kelogsloops Traverse the Emotional Terrain of Love and Loss
description: Conceptually, memento mori has been around for millennia. Ancient Greek philosophers like Socrates and Seneca reflected upon the nature of mortali
body:
Conceptually, memento mori has been around for millennia. Ancient Greek philosophers like Socrates and Seneca reflected upon the nature of mortality in ancient Greece. And during Roman triumphs, a handful of accounts document how a general would be accompanied by a companion or a slave who was tasked with reminding him he would eventually perish.
We often think of memento mori visually in relation to Dutch Golden Age paintings, where skulls or rotting fruit surrounded by insects served as reminders of the fleetingness of life. Latin for “remember you will die,” the phrase can be traced to a biblical passage. And for Melbourne-based artist Hieu Thien Nguyen, who works as kelogsloops, death is a constant reminder in fantastical, dreamlike watercolors.
“Koi No Yokan”
Often centering around a young woman with snow-white hair and repeating motifs like towering cumulus clouds, a black wolf, foxes, and other woodland creatures, kelogsloops’ paintings explore “the intensity of love, the inevitability of loss, and the quiet acceptance that comes with knowing nothing lasts forever,” says a statement for the artist’s forthcoming exhibition Love, Death, & All Her Friends at Corey Helford Gallery.
Emotions, and perhaps life forces, literally swirl through kelogsloops’ paintings via starlight, mist, and wind. Pieces like “The Waiting Room” and “The Carousel” suggest gentle, liminal spaces between the waking and sleeping world—reality and whatever else may be out there. Exploring the boundary between awareness and unconsciousness, “there is no bitterness,” the artist says, “but instead an honest look at what it means to love something, knowing it won’t last forever, but to find beauty in that anyway.”
Love, Death, & All Her Friends opens on September 19 and continues through October 24 in Los Angeles. Find more on the artist’s Instagram.
